name: The Gunpowder Mile

intro.lead: Ten stops round the old centre of Gdansk.
intro.body:
About a mile of walking, an hour. Seven stops ask a question you can only answer by looking at the thing in front of you. Three just need you standing in the right place.

All outdoors, all free.
intro.start: Start at the Upland Gate, the Brama Wyzynna, at the western end of the old town on Waly Jagiellonskie. It is the low stone gate with three carved shields on it, a few minutes from the main station.

outro:
That is the ten.

If you have any walking left, keep going north. Ten minutes that way is the Great Mill, a medieval flour factory the size of a church, standing on a canal that was dug by hand to drive it. Another ten minutes past that is the shipyard, and the shipyard is a walk of its own.

topics.name: Behind the Pretty Front
topics.blurb: A fortress gate, a shooting club and an arsenal, all dressed as something else.

topics.name: Not From Here
topics.blurb: The Dutch, the Flemish and the English who came for the money and left buildings behind.

topics.name: Clay, Water and Grain
topics.blurb: What this city had to hand, and what it built out of it.

stops.title: The Upland Gate
stops.where: Brama Wyzynna, Waly Jagiellonskie, at the western end of the old town

question.ask: One of those pairs has a single horn in the middle of its forehead. What are they?
question.hint: Look at the shield on the left as you face the gate. The two beasts holding it are not horses.

stops.look:
Stand back far enough to see the whole front of the gate.

Three carved shields run across it in a row, and each one is held up by a pair of animals. It is not the same animal on every shield, so look at all three.
stops.after:
Left to right, those are the arms of Royal Prussia held by unicorns, Poland held by angels, and Gdansk held by lions. Three rulers on one wall, in the order that mattered to whoever paid for the carving.

This is the start of the Royal Route. When a Polish king came to Gdansk he came in through this gate and walked straight down the main street to the river, past everything the city wanted him to see.

You are going to leave that route almost at once and go round the back of it.

The gate went up between 1574 and 1588, and the shields were added in 1586.

The two crosses on the Gdansk shield turn up everywhere once you have seen them. Manhole covers, lamp posts, bins.

stops.title: The Theatre on the Coal Market
stops.where: Gdanski Teatr Szekspirowski, ulica Boguslawskiego 1, just south of Targ Weglowy
stops.directions:
Face the old town with the Upland Gate behind you, then turn right and walk south along the edge of the ring road.

Take the first left, into ulica Boguslawskiego, and carry on east. About two hundred metres in all.

You cannot miss the building. It is tall, it has almost no windows, and it is the only thing in sight that does not look old.

question.hint: Hold it against the wall of anything else in sight. It is the opposite of every other building in this city.

stops.look:
Everything else you will look at today is red brick or painted plaster.

Get close enough to touch this one and look at the brick it is built from.
stops.after:
Black, and deliberately so. It was finished in 2014, designed by the Venetian architect Renato Rizzi, and the colour is there to set it against every red wall around it. There are said to be one point two million of those bricks.

It stands on the site of the Fencing School, a playhouse built here in 1635 on an English plan by a Flemish builder called Jakob van Blocke. That one replaced a theatre of 1610 where English actors were performing Shakespeare while Shakespeare was still alive.

Gdansk was on the circuit. Companies of English players came over for the fairs and worked their way round the Baltic ports, playing in a language most of the audience did not speak.

The roof of the new one opens, and it takes about three minutes to do it. On a warm night they slide it back and play under the sky, which is how it was done here in 1610.

Ian McKellen, Judi Dench and Kenneth Branagh all lent their names to the campaign that got it built.

stops.title: The Shooting Club
stops.where: Dwor Bractwa sw. Jerzego, at the top of Targ Weglowy beside the Golden Gate
stops.directions:
Walk back north, past the end of the theatre, until a long open square opens up on your left. This is Targ Weglowy, the Coal Market. About ninety metres.

At the near corner of it, tucked in beside the big ornamental gate into the old town, is a small square brick building. It has battlements along the top and little turrets hanging off its corners.

question.ask: What is he sticking it into?
question.hint: The rider is St George. There is only one animal he is remembered for.

stops.look:
Look at the very top of the little tower.

There is a man on horseback up there. His spear is pointing down at something underneath the horse.
stops.after:
A dragon, and the rider is St George.

This was the clubhouse of the Brotherhood of St George, which was a shooting club. The richest men in Gdansk met here to drink, do business and shoot at a wooden bird on a pole. Being a member was the point. The shooting was the excuse.

The building went up in the 1480s and the brotherhood used it until the end of the 1700s.

The George on the roof is a copy. The original is a sixteenth century figure and it is indoors at the National Museum, out of the weather.

He is also the patron saint of England. Shooting guilds all over northern Europe claimed him, and England claimed him for the same reason: he was the saint that fighting men prayed to.

stops.title: The Building That Is Pretending
stops.where: Wielka Zbrojownia, closing the eastern side of Targ Weglowy
stops.directions:
With the Golden Gate behind you on your right, walk north up the length of the Coal Market, about a hundred and ten metres.

Closing off the top end of the square is the most decorated building here, covered in carved stonework and gilding.

Stand well back so you can take in the width of the front in one go.

question.ask: How many separate houses does it look like?
question.hint: Count the pointed gables along the top. One gable, one house.

stops.look:
Look along the roofline.

Each gable sits above its own front door, its own row of windows and its own strip of wall, exactly like the merchant houses on any street in this city.
stops.after:
Four, and it is one building.

This is the Great Armoury. It was built between 1600 and 1605 to hold the city's guns, powder and armour, and the front was made to look like four merchant houses standing in a row.

The architect was Anthonis van Obbergen, from Mechelen in Flanders. He gave a weapons store the face of a shopping street.

Go round to the far side, on Piwna, and the pretence drops. That front has two octagonal towers and two great stone doorways with the city arms held up by lions, which is what a state arsenal is supposed to look like.

It burned in 1945 and took about eighteen years to put back. It is the Academy of Fine Arts now, so there are usually students on the steps.

stops.title: Beer Street
stops.where: ulica Piwna, running east from the Armoury towards the church
stops.directions:
Go through the archway in the middle of the Armoury, or round either end of it, and come out on the far side into a narrow street running east.

Walk down it about a hundred and sixty metres, until the church tower ahead of you fills the end of the street.

gate.prompt: Get into Piwna itself, somewhere near the middle, with the church tower ahead of you.

stops.look:
Stand in the middle of the road and look east.

Every other street in this city runs down to the water and finishes at a gate. This one finishes at a wall.
stops.after:
This is Piwna, which means beer.

Its old name was Jopejska, after Jopen beer: a dark, thick wheat beer that went abroad in barrels as a luxury. It was brewed on this street.

The beer was made from the same grain that made the city rich. It came down the Vistula from half of Poland, and what was not sold abroad got drunk.

The street stops at the church because the church is too big to go round. It takes up a whole block of the town, and the streets had to give way to it.

stops.title: Number 52, Broad Street
stops.directions:
Take the first turning on your left, going north, and cross straight over ulica sw. Ducha.

One street further north is ulica Szeroka, the Broad Street. Turn right along it and walk east about two hundred metres.

You want the house on the left with a restaurant on the ground floor and its name written up over the door.

question.hint: It swims up rivers, and it is in the name of the restaurant in both languages.

stops.look:
The house is named after an animal and the name is written over the door.

There should be one on the front of the building as well, carved or painted. Have a look for it.
stops.after:
A salmon.

In 1598 a Dutch Mennonite called Ambrosius Vermollen set up a distillery and an inn on this spot and called it Der Lachs, the Salmon. He was one of many Dutch protestants who came to Gdansk because the city let them worship as they liked and trade as they liked.

What he made here was Goldwasser: a clear spiced liqueur with flakes of real gold floating in it, twenty-two carat. The gold does nothing at all. It was thought to be good for you, and it looked like money.

It went to the courts of France, Sweden and Russia. The recipe has never been published.

The house burned in 1945 with the rest of the street. The family who rebuilt the restaurant have been running it since 1976.

A salmon.

stops.title: The One That Did Not Burn
stops.where: Brama Chlebnicka, on Dlugie Pobrzeze where ulica Chlebnicka reaches the water
stops.directions:
Carry on east to the end of Szeroka and turn right onto the waterfront path along the Motlawa.

Follow the river south about two hundred and fifty metres. The great timber crane is on your right almost at once.

Keep going until you reach a heavy brick gate on your right with a street running back into the town behind it. That street is Chlebnicka.

gate.prompt: Get to the Bread Gate on the waterfront, where Chlebnicka meets the quay.

stops.look:
Look up at the gate, then look along the quay in both directions.

There is another one like it at the end of every street that reaches the water.
stops.after:
Every street in the Main Town had its own gate onto its own stretch of quay, and the gates are named after what came through them. This is the Bread Gate. Along the same quay there is a Cow Gate and a Stall-keepers' Gate.

A street here was a business. The merchants who lived on it owned the wharf at the end of it, and the gate was where the city took its cut and locked up at night.

This one went up in the fifteenth century and it worked as a customs post and a water tower.

Almost everything you have looked at today was flattened in 1945 and put back afterwards. This gate came through the war with most of its gothic shape still on it. You are looking at the real thing.

stops.title: Number 16, Bread Street
stops.directions:
Go through the gate and walk west up Chlebnicka, away from the river, about seventy metres.

On your left is a house that does not fit. It is far wider and taller than anything on either side of it, with rows of flat stone columns running up the front.

question.ask: How many of those plots does it take up?
question.hint: Measure it by eye against the house next door. It is a whole number of them.

stops.look:
Look at the houses on either side of it first.

Every one is narrow. One door, two or three windows across, one steep gable. That is the standard plot on this street.

Now look at the wide one again.
stops.after:
Two.

It was built between 1568 and 1570 for Dirck Lylge, a merchant from Westphalia, who bought two plots and laid one house across both of them. The architect was Hans Kramer. It is about thirty metres tall with six floors, which made it one of the largest houses in the city.

It started as a cloth warehouse and shop. English merchants worked out of it, and by the eighteenth century it was a hotel the English liked, which is where the name comes from.

England and Gdansk were in constant traffic. English cloth came in, and much of the timber, tar and rope that built the English navy went out of the Baltic through ports like this one.

It was rebuilt after the war and belongs to the Academy of Fine Arts now, like the Armoury.

stops.title: The King's Chapel
stops.where: Kaplica Krolewska, ulica sw. Ducha 58, on the north side of the great church
stops.directions:
Keep going west up Chlebnicka to the end, then turn right and work your way north around the huge church that fills the view.

Come out onto ulica sw. Ducha and turn left. About a hundred and eighty metres in all.

On the right hand side of the street, wedged tight between two ordinary houses, is a small building with a dome on top of it.

gate.prompt: Get onto sw. Ducha, in front of the little domed chapel on the north side.

stops.look:
Everything around it is gothic brick. Flat fronts, straight lines, steep gables.

This is stone, and curves, and it has been squeezed into a gap that is plainly too small for it.
stops.after:
It was built between 1678 and 1681, paid for by King Jan III Sobieski, and the design is credited to his court architect Tylman van Gameren.

The great church next door had gone Lutheran in the 1570s and stayed that way for nearly four hundred years. Gdansk was a protestant city under a Catholic king, and it defended that arrangement hard.

So the Catholics of Gdansk had nowhere to go. The king could not take the big church back, so he bought a gap between two houses on this street and built them a chapel in it.

Two years after it was finished he broke the siege of Vienna.

stops.title: St Mary's
stops.where: Bazylika Mariacka, the church filling the whole block beside you
stops.directions:
Cross the street and walk about forty metres to the wall of the church itself.

Go right up to it, and get your back against something so you can look up.

question.ask: So what is it built of?
question.hint: Get close and look at the wall. It is not stone.

stops.look:
Look at the size of it first. Then walk right up and put your hand flat on the wall.

Every great cathedral you can name is built of cut stone. This one is not.
stops.after:
Brick. It is the largest brick church in the world, and depending on how you measure, one of the largest churches of any kind.

It is a hundred and five metres long and the inside will hold something like twenty thousand people. There is no building stone in this part of Poland, only clay, so the whole region built in brick and got very good at it.

It took about a hundred and sixty years to finish, from 1379 to 1502.

In 1945 the roof and the vaults burned and much of the inside was destroyed. The walls held. It was patched, then properly rebuilt, and the work went on for decades.

The Armoury, the house with the salmon, the English House and this church all burned in the same few weeks of one spring. Every one of them was put back by hand. The gate down on the waterfront is the only thing you stopped at today that did not need it.
